source: Graber, Franklin, Gordon (2005) Diagnostic error in internal medicine
finding: Case review of 100 diagnostic errors found cognitive causes in most cases, but also system causes. Cognitive-only errors were a minority.
numbers: 100 cases, 5 academic centers, 5 years (129 reviewed, 29 excluded). 38 wrong, 34 missed, 28 delayed diagnoses. 90 caused harm, 33 deaths. Cognitive factors in 74%, system factors 65%, no-fault 44%. Cognitive only 28%, system only 19%, both 46%, no-fault only 7%. Mean 5.9 factors per case (320 cognitive, 228 system).
limits: Cases came from QA reports (57), voluntary reports (33), autopsy discrepancies (10): selected, no denominator of all diagnoses. Consensus classification by 1 internist and 2 psychologists; no inter-rater figure read. Hindsight bias possible.
agent_relevance: The cognitive share is real but 65% of cases had system factors too. A thinking scaffold addresses only part of the error pool. Do not claim it removes most diagnostic error.

source: Graber, Franklin, Gordon (2005) Diagnostic error in internal medicine (cognitive breakdown)
finding: Within cognitive errors, faulty synthesis dominated. Premature closure was the single most common named item but only about 12% of cognitive instances. Knowledge gaps were rare.
numbers: Of 320 cognitive instances: faulty synthesis 264 (~83%), faulty data gathering 45 (~14%), premature closure 39 (~12%, listed within synthesis group), knowledge or skill deficits 11 (~3%; knowledge 4, skill 7). Percentages computed from reported counts.
limits: Counts overlap by taxonomy (subcategories sum to 265 for synthesis). Reviewers judged cause after the fact. 'Knowledge is rarely the problem' can reflect how causes were coded.
agent_relevance: Errors are mostly in putting known facts together (synthesis, closure), not missing facts. This supports scaffolds that force alternatives and recheck, over adding retrieval. It is a single-center-set, retrospective source.

source: Norman, Monteiro, Sherbino, Ilgen, Schmidt, Mamede (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking
finding: Review concludes both fast (Type 1) and slow (Type 2) reasoning cause errors. Biases can be induced in the lab (availability best shown), but their real contribution to errors is not well established. Bias-recognition teaching does not reduce errors. Knowledge reorganisation gives small but consistent gains.
numbers: No pooled effect size. Narrative review.
quote: Educational strategies directed at the recognition of biases are ineffective in reducing errors
limits: Narrative, not meta-analysis. Authors are leading proponents of the knowledge-deficit view (rival camp to Croskerry). Read at abstract level.
agent_relevance: Strong warning for the not-to-add list: a 'list of named biases' prompt is the analogue of bias-recognition teaching and has weak human evidence. Prefer structural moves (generate rivals, re-derive from raw findings).

source: Saposnik, Redelmeier, Ruff, Tobler (2016) Cognitive biases associated with medical decisions: a systematic review
finding: Systematic review: every included study found some bias or trait affecting physicians. Overconfidence, anchoring, information and availability bias linked to diagnostic inaccuracy in 36.5 to 77% of case scenarios. Evidence for patient outcome effects is almost absent.
numbers: 20 studies, 6810 physicians, 19 biases, from 114 publications (MEDLINE and Cochrane 1980 to May 2015). 5 of 7 (71.4%) studies linked bias to management errors. Only 2 of 20 (10%) studied patient outcomes; 1 showed effect (complications 9.7% vs 6.5%, p=.004). 12 of 20 (60%) rated low quality. Only 5 (25%) used guidelines as the error standard.
limits: No pooled effect. Mostly vignettes. Heterogeneous bias definitions. Publication bias likely (all studies found something).
agent_relevance: Bias effects are real in vignettes but patient-level harm from bias per se is barely measured. Treat bias lists as hypotheses, not proven drivers.

source: Sherbino, Kulasegaram, Howey, Norman (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning: a controlled trial
finding: Training medical students in cognitive forcing strategies did not improve cases prone to search-satisficing or availability bias.
numbers: 191 students (145 trained, 46 control). Search-satisficing cases: second diagnosis sought by 52% vs 48% (p=.91); correct second diagnosis 54% vs 48% (p=.13). False-positive cases: 64% vs 77% over-identified (p=.12). Availability cases: 45% vs 45% found the uncommon diagnosis (p=.98).
limits: Novices only. Not randomised individually (allocated by rotation block), unequal groups. Authorship attribution from memory; PubMed page gives title and results. Training format may have been weak.
agent_relevance: Instructing a reasoner to 'force' alternatives did nothing for novices. A scaffold must do the work (explicit generated rival set), not rely on the reasoner's reminding itself.

source: Mamede et al. (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents (JAMA)
finding: Prior exposure to similar cases lowered accuracy in second-year residents (availability bias) but not first-years. Structured reflection (re-analysis of findings) improved accuracy on those cases in both years.
numbers: 36 residents (18 PGY1, 18 PGY2). PGY2: 1.55 (CI 1.15-1.96) on similar-to-prior cases vs 2.19 (1.73-2.66) on others (p=.03). PGY1 showed the opposite pattern (2.03 vs 1.42, p=.046). PGY2 gave the earlier, biased diagnosis 1.44 vs 0.72 times (p=.04). Reflection: PGY2 2.03 (1.49-2.57), PGY1 2.31 (1.89-2.73) (p=.006). Max score 4.0.
limits: Small N, single site, no main effects, only interaction. Reflection was always second (order confounded with time/extra processing). Availability is not anchoring/closure, but the cleanest induced-bias result.
agent_relevance: Reflection means re-working the case from findings, not just 'think again'. This is the best human support for a recheck state, and it targets induced bias.

source: Lambe, O'Reilly, Kelly, Curristan (2016) Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review
finding: 28 studies of interventions. Guided reflection was the most consistently successful (5 studies). Cognitive forcing improved accuracy and confidence judgments. Measurement was very heterogeneous and samples mostly early-career.
numbers: 28 studies, five categories: education, checklists, cognitive forcing, guided reflection, instructions at test. No pooled effect size.
limits: Narrative synthesis. Conflicts with the null forcing results (b05). Mostly trainees. Read at abstract level.
agent_relevance: If one intervention is kept, guided reflection (structured re-analysis) has the best human record. Forcing and checklists are mixed.

source: Monteiro, Sherbino, Sibbald, Norman et al. (2015) Reflecting on diagnostic errors: taking a second look is not enough (J Gen Intern Med)
finding: When residents were free to reconsider their own diagnoses, they revised few and gained almost nothing.
numbers: 47 residents (PGY1-3), 16 cases. Only 8% of diagnoses revised. Score rose 1.20 to 1.22 out of 2 (t=2.15, p=.03). Revised at least one: 12/19 PGY1, 9/11 PGY2, 8/17 PGY3. Pass-1 means 1.17, 1.35, 1.27.
limits: Author list from memory (not verified on the page). Self-directed reflection, unlike the experimenter-controlled version in b06. Residents often lack the knowledge to fix errors.
agent_relevance: A free-form 'look again' step does little. If the second look is not structured and does not bring new information, expect near-zero gain.

source: Monteiro, Norman et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning (Acad Med)
finding: Telling residents to be fast or to be careful made no difference to accuracy. Slow diagnoses were not better; wrong ones took longer.
numbers: 204 second-year residents (96 Speed in 2010, 108 Reflect in 2011), 20 internal medicine cases. Accuracy 44.5% vs 45.0% (n.s.). Time 69 s vs 89 s (p<.001). Incorrect cases took ~17 s longer. Accuracy correlated with licensing exam scores and inversely with time.
limits: Cohorts were different years (not concurrent randomisation). Instruction-only manipulation; accuracy low (45%) so floor effects possible. Author order not verified.
agent_relevance: Instruction to slow down is not a mechanism. Argues against a generic 'think carefully' prompt line as a debiaser. Knowledge limited accuracy.

source: Ilgen, Bowen, McIntyre et al. (2013) Comparing diagnostic performance and the utility of clinical vignette-based assessment under testing conditions designed to encourage either automatic or analytic thought
finding: Large randomised comparison: first-impression instructions and directed-search instructions gave the same accuracy.
numbers: 393 clinicians (students, trainees, faculty). Instruction effect F(1,379)=2.44, p=.12. Vignette complexity F=965.2 and experience F=39.6 both p<.001.
limits: Accuracy outcome only. Complexity and experience dwarf instruction. Authors not fully verified from page.
agent_relevance: Case difficulty and knowledge dominate. Process instructions move accuracy little, so test any scaffold step against a plain baseline.

source: Debiasing versus knowledge retrieval checklists to reduce diagnostic error in ECG interpretation (2020, Adv Health Sci Educ)
finding: Neither a debiasing checklist nor a knowledge checklist beat control, even on ECGs deliberately built to induce bias. Bias-built cases did cause more errors.
numbers: 61 participants: 40 novice PGY1, 21 cardiology fellows, 3 arms, 20 ECGs (half bias-prone). Bias cases more errors F=96.9, p<.0001. No checklist effect; no checklist-by-level interaction. Authors say it may help novices.
limits: Authors not verified from page. Small cells. ECG reading is perceptual-knowledge heavy.
agent_relevance: A debiasing checklist in the scaffold has no human proof of benefit. Keep the induced-bias effect (large) separate from the debiasing effect (null).

source: Checklists to prevent diagnostic errors: a pilot randomized controlled trial (Diagnosis journal, differential-diagnosis checklist)
finding: Real-patient pilot: a read-aloud differential checklist raised the number of diagnoses considered but did not significantly cut error.
numbers: 14 primary care physicians, 100 patients. 17 errors. Error rate 11.2% checklist vs 17.8% usual (p=.46). Post-hoc emergency physicians 19.1% vs 45.0% (p=.04). Diagnoses considered 6.5 (SD 4.2) vs 3.4 (SD 2.0), p<.001.
limits: Pilot, tiny clusters, post-hoc subgroup. Year shown in index is 2022; trial likely earlier. Underpowered.
agent_relevance: Widening the differential is easy to produce (almost double) but its link to fewer errors is unproven. Do not count 'more hypotheses' as success.

source: Factors underlying suboptimal diagnostic performance in physicians under time pressure (Med Educ, ~2018)
finding: Time pressure lowered accuracy, partly through fewer alternative hypotheses and more stress.
numbers: 75 senior IM residents (40 pressure, 35 none), 8 cases. Time 85.5 s vs 181.8 s (p<.001). Accuracy 0.44 vs 0.53 (p=.01). Alternatives 0.37 vs 0.51 (p=.01). Path: pressure to alternatives beta=-0.32 (p<.01); pressure to stress beta=0.25 (p=.029).
limits: Mediation was post hoc. Written cases, not real care. Authors not verified from page.
agent_relevance: Fewer rival hypotheses is a measured mechanism of early stopping. Supports tracking rival-set size as a state variable. A compute budget in an agent is the analogue of time pressure.

source: Time pressure in diagnosing written clinical cases: an experimental study on time constraints and perceived time pressure (2025)
finding: Actual time limit lowered accuracy; the feeling of time pressure did not. Both affected confidence.
numbers: US residents, online within-subject. Restricted time limit: lower accuracy (p=.044). Perceived pressure on accuracy: n.s. Confidence: actual limit p=.012, perceived pressure p=.048. Limit set at mean plus or minus 1 SD.
limits: N and effect size not in abstract. p=.044 is borderline. Partial replication of b13.
agent_relevance: The cost comes from real limits on work done, not from mindset. For an agent: real reasoning budget matters, telling it to hurry may not.

source: Failure to demonstrate effects of interruptions on diagnostic reasoning: three experiments (2022)
finding: Three experiments found no accuracy cost of interruptions, a failed test of a popular error-cause claim.
numbers: Exp 1 N=42: 0.88 vs 0.91. Exp 2 N=78: 0.95 vs 0.94. Exp 3 N=30 with time pressure: 0.42 vs 0.37. More time needed when interrupted, significant only in Exp 2.
limits: Small N, ceiling in Exp 1 and 2. Absence of effect is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Not every observed error cause is causal in experiments. Be cautious adding guardrails for causes shown only by observation.

source: Berner & Graber (2008) Overconfidence as a cause of diagnostic error in medicine (Am J Med)
finding: Review argues physicians underestimate the chance their diagnosis is wrong, which supports premature closure. Covers incidence, overconfidence data, and strategies.
numbers: No pooled numbers in abstract.
quote: physicians in general underappreciate the likelihood that their diagnoses are wrong
limits: Narrative, abstract only read. Overlaps with the parallel calibration subfield.
agent_relevance: Links closure to confidence: a stop rule based on stated confidence is itself biased. Calibration is covered in the Calibration subfield.

source: Premature closure underlies bias in medical diagnosis in students: a randomised controlled experiment (2026)
finding: First direct behavioural evidence of premature closure: biasing findings placed early cut accuracy and cut processing time per word. Late placement cut accuracy less, with no time change. This favours early stopping over hypothesis competition.
numbers: 58 fourth-year students, 12 vignettes. Accuracy 0.27 no distractor vs 0.11 distractor at start (61% drop; F(2,693)=11.995, p<.001) vs 0.17 at end (36% drop). Time per word fell only for early distractor (F(2,636)=4.799, p<.01).
quote: Premature closure can therefore be directly observed rather than inferred
limits: Students, not physicians. Low base accuracy (0.27). Time per word is an indirect proxy for stopping.
agent_relevance: Order matters: early salient findings do the damage. For an agent, a scaffold step that re-reads the case in a different order, or hides the anchor, is mechanistically motivated.

source: Cognitive mechanisms underlying anchoring bias in diagnosis: a randomized controlled experiment (2026, Brazilian residents, eye tracking)
finding: Eye tracking: residents looked at distractors and key discriminating findings equally, whether right or wrong. The difference was in what they remembered: right answers recalled more key findings and fewer distractors.
numbers: Recall of discriminating features 0.47 (CI 0.40-0.53) accurate vs 0.20 (0.06-0.33) distractor-led. Recall of distractors 0.16 (0.08-0.24) vs 0.37 (0.24-0.50). 6 vignettes, 3 versions, crossover. Fixation counts did not differ.
limits: N not in abstract. Recall is post hoc and may reflect the final diagnosis, not cause it.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is not missing the data; it is weighing it wrong. A scaffold should force explicit scoring of each finding against each rival, not just ask the model to look at everything.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA)
finding: Seven induced cognitive biases (including recency, frequency, confirmation, false consensus, status quo, cultural, self-diagnosis) lowered accuracy on USMLE-style items in every model tested. GPT-4 was the most robust; weaker models lost much more.
numbers: Baseline accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7b 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-LLaMA-13b 33.4%. Overall drop 10 to 26% across models. GPT-4 worst case false consensus -14.0%, confirmation only -0.2%. GPT-3.5 average -37.4%, worst 23.9% accuracy. Mean over models: false consensus -24.9%, frequency -18.2%, recency -12.9%, confirmation -8.1%.
limits: Bias is a sentence inserted in a MedQA stem, a crude stand-in for clinical anchoring. Authors say simulating bias this way is very challenging. No anchoring-on-early-diagnosis or premature closure arm. Non-response rates differed by model.
agent_relevance: The only large LLM benchmark of this type. Cheap prompt-injected opinions move LLMs a lot (social bias more than confirmation). Test our scaffold on it as a robustness check, not as proof of closure repair.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models: mitigation strategies
finding: Three prompt fixes (bias education text, one-shot negative example, few-shot negative plus positive examples) helped only modestly, and mostly for GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-4 frequency bias 0.627 to 0.720 with education. GPT-4 recency 0.679 to 0.742 with one-shot. Mixtral and GPT-3.5 only marginal gains. Authors call gains modest and below the no-bias level.
limits: Single run per cell as far as read; no confidence intervals read. Education prompt is a short warning, not a structured procedure.
agent_relevance: A 'be aware of bias' prompt line is the weakest debiaser in LLMs too, matching human nulls (b05, b11). Do not add one. Worked examples helped slightly more.

source: Qazi et al. (2025) Automation bias in LLM-assisted diagnostic reasoning among AI-trained physicians: a randomized clinical trial (medRxiv; published NEJM AI 2026)
finding: Physicians who had a 20-hour AI-literacy course still lost accuracy when ChatGPT-4o advice contained deliberate errors (anchoring on the machine's answer).
numbers: 44 physicians (22 vs 22), 6 vignettes, 3 of 6 with erroneous advice in treatment. Reasoning score 84.9% (SD 19.7) vs 73.3% (SD 30.5); adjusted difference -14.0 points (95% CI -19.7 to -8.3, P<.0001). Top-choice accuracy 90.5% vs 76.1%; adjusted -18.3 points (CI -26.6 to -10.0).
limits: Preprint (single-blind, Pakistan, vignettes). Errors were deliberately planted by physicians. Voluntary use. Single session. No mitigation arm.
agent_relevance: The anchor can be an LLM's output. A multi-agent or self-critique design that passes a first answer forward can import this same bias. Input answers should be treated as claims, not facts.

source: Qazi et al. (2026) Mitigating automation bias in physician-LLM diagnostic reasoning using behavioral nudges: a randomized controlled trial (medRxiv)
finding: A nudge showing benchmark accuracy plus a per-case ensemble-agreement traffic light raised reasoning scores in physicians using ChatGPT-5.1 advice with planted errors.
numbers: 72 physicians (36 vs 36), 432 cases. Mean 82.8% (SD 24.7) vs 75.6% (SD 28.7); adjusted +7.6 points (95% CI 1.4 to 13.9, P=0.016). Top-choice 79.5 vs 69.1; adjusted +10.9 points. Advice panel opened in 91.7% vs 93.5% of cases (n.s.).
limits: Preprint, single-blind vignettes, no component isolation (two cues bundled). CI lower bound near zero. Same research group as b21.
agent_relevance: Selective scrutiny (flag only where independent models disagree) worked without extra friction on every case. Supports disagreement among samples as a trigger for a recheck step, rather than always-on checking.

source: Goh et al. (2025) Physician clinical decision modification and bias assessment in a randomized controlled trial of AI assistance (Commun Med)
finding: When GPT-4 advice was correct, 50 physicians moved toward it and improved, with no extra demographic bias.
numbers: 50 US physicians, chest-pain video vignettes. Accuracy 47% to 65% (white male) and 63% to 80% (Black female); both about +18 points. Pre-post design.
limits: Pre-post, not parallel control; advice was good. Not an anchoring test.
agent_relevance: Benefit and harm from AI advice are the same mechanism (deference). Quality of the first answer decides which one occurs.

source: Large language models exhibit greater diagnostic anchoring than physicians in a forced-choice vignette study (SSRN 2026)
finding: Title found in Semantic Scholar listing only. Reports LLMs show more anchoring than physicians in forced-choice vignettes. Could not open (SSRN blocked).
numbers: Not read.
limits: Unopened; do not cite numbers. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Most directly on target for LLM anchoring; fetch full text through another route before relying on it.

source: Dialogical AI for cognitive bias mitigation in medical diagnosis (Applied Sciences 2026)
finding: Title found in Semantic Scholar listing only. A dialogue-based AI aimed at reducing clinician cognitive bias. Page returned 403.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Unopened. No claims should be made.
agent_relevance: Candidate comparator for challenge-by-dialogue designs; needs a read.

source: Qazi et al. (2025) automation bias trial: design details and limitations
finding: Authors list the main boundary conditions: vignettes only, deliberately planted (probably more obvious) errors, single session, one LLM, and no mitigation tested. They also cite older work where wrong AI predictions led pathologists to overturn correct diagnoses in 7% of cases.
numbers: Single-blind RCT 20 June to 15 August 2025; 75-minute sessions; 3 blinded physician raters with expert rubric.
limits: The 7% figure is a secondhand citation (not opened).
agent_relevance: Effect sizes here are upper-bound style: planted errors in half of cases. Real error rates are lower, so net harm varies with the model's true accuracy.

source: Qazi et al. (2026) nudge trial discussion: forcing functions and friction
finding: Authors argue always-on forcing functions (commit-first, fixed delays) add friction to every case and are poorly tolerated, and that uniform skepticism erodes the benefit of correct AI advice on routine cases.
numbers: No new numbers; argument based on refs 37 and 58 (not opened).
limits: Discussion claim, not tested in this trial; no component isolation.
agent_relevance: Supports conditional rather than always-on recheck states in the scaffold: spend extra reasoning only on flagged cases.
